title: Va'era: four promises (Exodus 6:6–7)
hook: I will bring out, deliver, redeem and take; the four cups of the seder

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Shemot: Moses shouts, why hast thou dealt ill, and God answers. Your line was you can say it. Did you name one real frustration? Today, a new portion, and the rest of God's answer. Day two hundred twenty-six.

If you've ever been to a Passover seder, you know there's wine. A lot of it, or grape juice, poured four separate times, at set points in the evening. Kids count the cups. Grandparents mutter about the fourth one. Some families set an extra cup in the middle of the table that nobody drinks, and open the door for it later in the night. Why four? Why the fifth? The answer isn't in the Passover story itself. It's in a few lines God says to Moses, right after Moses's angry complaint. Today: four promises.
screen: `WINE AT THE SEDER.` → `FOUR CUPS, COUNTED.` → `A FIFTH CUP NOBODY DRINKS.`

segments.voice: This portion is called Va'era, and I appeared, from God's words: I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Then God gives Moses a message for the people, and it comes as a chain of verbs. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians." I will deliver you from their bondage. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm. And: "I will take you to Me for a people." Four verbs. In Hebrew, vehotzeti, vehitzalti, vega'alti, velakachti. Bring out, deliver, redeem, take. Notice they build. First, out from under the burden: the work stops. Then out of slavery itself. Then redeemed, bought back, restored. And last, not just free from something, but taken toward someone: you'll be my people. Freedom isn't only escape. It ends in belonging. The rabbis of the Jerusalem Talmud connected these four verbs to the four cups of wine at the seder. One cup for each promise. So every Passover, families drink their way, slowly, through this verse. And the fifth cup? The very next verse has a fifth promise: I will bring you in, to the land. Some texts of the Talmud mention a fifth cup, and later sages debated it. One popular explanation is that the question was left for the prophet Elijah to settle someday, so a cup is poured for him, and nobody drinks it. Four promises kept at the table, and one still waiting at the door.
screen: `VA'ERA — AND I APPEARED.` · `OUT, DELIVER, REDEEM, TAKE.` · `ONE CUP FOR EACH PROMISE.` · `THE FIFTH CUP WAITS FOR ELIJAH.` · then, large: `FOUR CUPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name four freedoms you have. Settle, and breathe. Count them on your fingers, one per breath or so. One burden you've been brought out from. One thing you're free of that once held you. One thing that was restored to you. And one place or person you belong to now. They can be small: a debt paid, a habit dropped, a friendship repaired, a table where you're welcome. Four cups. The bell holds the time.
Va'era. And I appeared. The portion where God promises four things, bring out, deliver, redeem, take, and the seder gives each a cup.
Your line: four cups. Today, when you drink something, a coffee, a glass of water, name one freedom you have before you sip. Day two hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: At the Passover seder, each participant drinks four cups of wine or grape juice at set points in the evening, and a cup is customarily poured for Elijah, with the door opened for him near the end of the meal.

original.note: Hebrew: four cups. The four cups of the Passover seder.

what it means: each cup at the seder answers one of God's four promises in Exodus 6.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 6:6 and 6:7 fragments.
Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 10:1 (four cups for the four expressions of redemption; Genesis Rabbah 88:5 also) from memory; confirm.
Fifth cup: some versions of Pesachim 118a mention a fifth cup; the link to Elijah's cup (teiku, Elijah will settle it) is a popular explanation, presented as such. Confirm framing.
Transliterations vehotzeti, vehitzalti, vega'alti, velakachti: confirm.
